cmimc-2018-numbertheory-01.title: Eliminate c
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-01.body:
The equations say $2c=a-2b$ and $3c=b-3a$. Eliminating $c$: $3(a-2b)=2(b-3a)$, so $9a=8b$. Since $\gcd(a,b)$ divides $c$ too and the triple is coprime, $(a,b)=\pm(8,9)$. Then $2c=8-18=-10$, so $c=\mp5$. Check: $\frac{8}{9-5}=2$ and $\frac{9}{8-5}=3$ ✓.

**Answer: 5**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-02.title: Factor and bound
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-02.body:
For $n\le0$, $(n-1)2^n$ is an integer only for $n\ge-1$ (for $n\le-2$ the odd number $n-1$ is not divisible by $2^{-n}\ge4$, so the expression is not an integer). Checking: $n=0$ gives $-1+1=0=0^2$ and $n=-1$ gives $-2\cdot\frac12+1=0=0^2$. Both work.

Now let $n>0$ and $x^2=(n-1)2^n+1$, so $(x-1)(x+1)=(n-1)2^n$. Since $\gcd(x-1,x+1)\le2$, one of $x\pm1$ is divisible by $2^{n-1}$.

- If $2^{n-1}\mid x-1$ with $x-1\ge2^{n-1}$, then $x+1\le2(n-1)$ (because the product is $(n-1)2^n$ and the other factor is then at most $2(n-1)$), so $2=(x+1)-(x-1)\le2(n-1)-2^{n-1}$, which is impossible for $n>4$.
- If $2^{n-1}\mid x+1$, then $2=(x+1)-(x-1)\ge2^{n-1}-2(n-1)>2$ for $n>4$, again impossible.

So $n\le4$; testing $n=1,2,3,4$: $1$, $5$, $17$, $49$; the squares are $n=1$ ($1$) and $n=4$ ($49=7^2$).

Hence $n=-1,0,1,4$.

**Answer: $n=-1,0,1,4$**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-03.title: Parity and powers of 2
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-03.body:
If $n\in S$ is even then $4\mid n$, so $n+1\equiv1\pmod 4$ and $n+1\notin S$ (an element of $S$ is divisible by $4$ or is $\equiv7\pmod 8$, hence is never $\equiv1\pmod4$). So $n$ is odd, hence $n\equiv7\pmod 8$ and $n+1\equiv0\pmod 8$. Then $n+1=4^a(8b+7)$ with $a\ge2$, so $n+1\ge16\cdot7=112$ and $n\ge111$.

$n=111=8\cdot13+7\in S$ and $n+1=112=4^2\cdot7\in S$. So $n=111$.

**Answer: 111**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-04.title: Work backwards
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-04.body:
If $a=2$ the sequence is $2,3,2,\dots$, so to have seven distinct terms the sequence must end at $a_7=2$ with $a_6\ge3$ (no integer $a\ge4$ has $a^2-1$ a power of $2$, so $2$ is reached only from $3$). All $a_n$ with $n\ge2$ are primes. Since $a_{n+1}\mid(a_n-1)(a_n+1)$ with $a_n$ an odd prime (both factors even), $a_{n+1}\le\frac{a_n+1}2$, so $a_n\ge2a_{n+1}-1$. Eventually the sequence must reach $2$ or $3$ ($a_n=3\to 2\to 3$) so to have 7 distinct terms we need $a_7=2$, $a_6=3$ at best: $a_6\ge3$. Then

$$a_2\ge2a_3-1\ge4a_4-3\ge8a_5-7\ge16a_6-15\ge33.$$

Primes between $33$ and $47$ give chains that are too short (e.g. $37\to19\to3\to2$, $41\to5\to3\to2$, $43\to7\to3\to2$). For $47$: $47^2-1=46\cdot48$, largest prime $23$; $23\to11$ ($22\cdot24$); $11\to5$; $5\to3$; $3\to2$. So $47,23,11,5,3,2$ are distinct. This gives $a_2=47$ as the smallest possible value of $a_2$.

Finally, $a_2\le a_1+1$ (largest prime factor of $(a_1-1)(a_1+1)$), so $a_1\ge a_2-1\ge46$. And $a_1=46$ works since $46^2-1=45\cdot47$.

Thus $a=46$ with the sequence $46,47,23,11,5,3,2$.

**Answer: 46**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-05.title: Few jumps
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-05.body:
Since $m_i\ge i-1$, and $\binom{102}{100}=5151>2018$, we need $m_{100}\le101$. Write $m_i=i-1,i,$ or $i+1$ (the sequence $m_i-i$ is non-decreasing from $-1$ and bounded by $1$). So for some $1\le a\le b\le100$: $m_i=i-1$ for $i\le a$, $m_i=i$ for $a<i\le b$, $m_i=i+1$ for $i>b$.

Using $\binom{i-1}{i}=0$, $\binom ii=1$, $\binom{i+1}{i}=i+1$:

$$2018=(b-a)+\sum_{i=b+1}^{100}(i+1)=b-a+\frac{101\cdot102}{2}-\frac{(b+1)(b+2)}{2}.$$

Simplifying, $3132=\frac{b^2+b}{2}+a$. With $b\approx\sqrt{6264}\approx79$ we try $b=78$: $\frac{78\cdot79}2=3081$ and $a=51$ ✓ (within $1\le a\le b$). 

Then the sum is $\sum_{i\le51}(i-1)+\sum_{i=52}^{78}i+\sum_{i=79}^{100}(i+1)=\frac{100\cdot101}2-51+22=5021$.

**Answer: 5021**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-06.title: Characterise
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-06.body:
Claim: for $n>1$, $\phi(n)\mid n$ iff $n=2^a3^b$ with $a\ge1$, $b\ge0$. Indeed $n$ must be even, and writing $n=2^am$ with $m$ odd, every odd prime $p\mid m$ contributes a factor $p-1$ to $\phi(n)$ and the power of $2$ in $\phi(n)$ would exceed $a$ unless $m$ has at most one prime factor $p$ with $p-1=2$, so $p=3$. (If $m$ had two odd primes, or a prime with $4\mid p-1$, then $2^{a+1}\mid\phi(n)\mid n$, a contradiction.)

The numbers $2^a3^b<100$, $a\ge1$: $b=0$: $2+4+8+16+32+64=126$; $b=1$: $6+12+24+48+96=186$; $b=2$: $18+36+72=126$; $b=3$: $54$. Total $126+186+126+54=492$.

**Answer: 492**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-07.title: Order of 16
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-07.body:
For $n=2^em$ with $m$ odd, $\pi(1/n)$ is the multiplicative order of $16$ modulo $m$ (the power of $2$ only affects the pre-period). Since $16=2^4$, this order is the smallest $k$ with $2^{4k}\equiv1\pmod m$, at most $\frac{\varphi(m)}{2}$: indeed $\varphi(m)$ is even (for $m>2$), so $16^{\varphi(m)/2}=2^{2\varphi(m)}=(2^{\varphi(m)})^2\equiv1\pmod m$. Hence $\pi\le\frac{m-1}{2}\le33$ for $m\le67$.

For $m=69=3\cdot23$: $16^{11}\equiv1\pmod{69}$, so $\pi\le11$. For $m\le70$ other values are smaller.

For $m=67$ (prime), $2$ is a primitive root mod $67$ (check $2^{33},2^{22},2^6\not\equiv1$), so $\operatorname{ord}_{67}(2)=66$ and $\operatorname{ord}_{67}(16)=66/\gcd(66,4)=33$.

**Answer: 33**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-08.title: Use the sum of cubes identity
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-08.body:
$p^3+q^3+r^3-3pqr=(p+q+r)(p^2+q^2+r^2-pq-qr-rp)$. With $p^3+q^3+r^3=249(p+q+r)$:

$$3pqr=(p+q+r)\bigl(249+pq+qr+rp-p^2-q^2-r^2\bigr).$$

The left side is a product of three primes, so $p+q+r$ divides $3pqr$. Since $p+q+r>3$ and $p+q+r>p,q,r$, it is a product of at least two primes from $\{3,p,q,r\}$; the case that works is $p+q+r=3q$ (found by trying the possibilities; the other cases give no solution). Then $p+r=2q$ and $3pqr=3q\cdot F$ requires $F=pr$, where $F=249+pq+qr+rp-p^2-q^2-r^2$. Since $q(p+r)=2q^2$, this simplifies to $249+q^2-p^2-r^2=0$. With $q=\frac{p+r}2$ this gives $3p^2-2pr+3r^2=996$. Mod $3$ this forces $3\mid 2pr$, so $p=3$ (as $p<r$ primes), and then $27-6r+3r^2=996$, i.e. $r^2-2r-323=0$, $r=19$ and $q=11$.

Check: $27+1331+6859=8217=249\cdot33$ ✓.

**Answer: 19**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-08.title: Bound and check
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-08.body: Since $249(p+q+r)=p^3+q^3+r^3$ and $r^3<249\cdot3r$, we get $r^2<747$, $r\le23$. A quick check of the primes up to $23$ gives only $(3,11,19)$.

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-09.title: Lambert series
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-09.body:
Let $x=\frac15$. Then $\frac1{x^{-n}+1}=\frac{x^n}{1+x^n}=\frac{x^n}{1-x^n}-\frac{2x^{2n}}{1-x^{2n}}$. We know $\sum_n\frac{\phi(n)t^n}{1-t^n}=\sum_n\phi(n)\sum_{m\ge1}t^{nm}=\sum_{s\ge1}\Bigl(\sum_{d\mid s}\phi(d)\Bigr)t^s=\sum_s st^s=\frac t{(1-t)^2}$.

Hence the sum is $\frac x{(1-x)^2}-2\frac{x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}=\frac{x(1+x^2)}{(1-x^2)^2}$. At $x=\frac15$: $\frac{\frac15\cdot\frac{26}{25}}{\left(\frac{24}{25}\right)^2}=\frac{26/125}{576/625}=\frac{26\cdot5}{576}=\frac{65}{288}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{65}{288}$**

cmimc-2018-numbertheory-10.title: Discriminant of the cyclotomic polynomial
cmimc-2018-numbertheory-10.body:
$S^2$ equals (up to sign) the discriminant of $\Phi_{91}$: $|S|^2=\prod_{p\ne q}|\omega^{a_p}-\omega^{a_q}|=\prod_i|\Phi_{91}'(\omega^{a_i})|$. Using $\Phi_{91}(x)=\frac{(x^{91}-1)(x-1)}{(x^7-1)(x^{13}-1)}$ and evaluating the derivative at the roots, then using $\prod_i(1-\omega^{a_i})=\Phi_{91}(1)=1$, $\prod(1-\omega^{7a_i})=\Phi_{13}(1)^6=13^6$, $\prod(1-\omega^{13a_i})=\Phi_7(1)^{12}=7^{12}$ and $\prod\omega^{a_i}=1$, we get

$$|S|^2=\frac{91^{72}}{7^{12}\,13^{6}}=7^{60}\,13^{66}.$$

So $S=7^{30}\cdot13^{33}$, which has $(30+1)(33+1)=31\cdot34=1054$ positive divisors. (A numerical check of $\ln|S|$ gives $143.02=30\ln7+33\ln13$.)

**Answer: 1054**
